issues.legal_issue: A housing authority cannot enforce a combined additional demand for development-related costs and increased land-acquisition compensation when the agreement requires the development-related price to be fixed within a specified time, but it may make a separate demand for the increased compensation.
material_facts: The allotment agreement required the authority to fix the price for development charges, amenities, buildings, and related costs within three years of allotment, while allowing revision for excess compensation finally awarded for the acquired land.
The authority made additional demands more than a decade after allotment, combining increased land-acquisition compensation with development-related costs without stating the amounts separately.
The High Court enjoined enforcement of the combined demand but allowed the authority to determine and separately demand the increased compensation; the Supreme Court agreed.
issues.conclusion: The injunction against the combined demand was upheld because the development-related amount had not been fixed within the contractual time and the demand did not separate that amount from increased land compensation. The authority could make a fresh, separate demand for increased land-acquisition compensation.
issues.legal_principle: The allotment agreement required development-related charges to be fixed within three years, while permitting revision for excess compensation finally awarded for acquired land. The authority could not use that compensation exception to recover development-related costs through a belated, unsegregated demand; it could separately seek the increased compensation. No earlier case or statutory provision was relied on for this contractual issue.

rule.if: housing_allotment_price_dispute and contract_required_timely_development_cost_calculation and development_costs_demanded_after_deadline and demand_combined_unsegregated_components

predicates.housing_allotment_price_dispute: The proceeding concerns additional prices or charges demanded by a housing authority from property allottees.
predicates.contract_required_timely_development_cos: The allotment agreement required development-related costs to be fixed within a specified period.
predicates.development_costs_demanded_after_deadlin: The authority demanded development-related costs after the contractual period for fixing them had expired.
predicates.demand_combined_unsegregated_components: The authority combined development-related costs and increased land-acquisition compensation in a demand without stating them separately.

issues.definition: When a housing authority makes a late, combined demand despite an agreement requiring timely calculation of development costs, the combined demand is enjoined, while a separate demand for increased land compensation remains permitted.

issues.legal_issue: A representative suit may proceed where the persons represented share a common interest or grievance, even if they have separate causes of action.
material_facts: The suit was brought on behalf of low-income allottees in the same colony who had received allotments under the same housing scheme and materially identical lease terms.
The challenged demands rested on the same basis for all the represented allottees, and the plaintiff's plea was available to them.
The authority argued that separate demands gave rise to separate causes of action and required separate suits.
The trial court permitted the representative suit, and the Supreme Court upheld that decision.
issues.conclusion: The suit was maintainable as a representative suit because the allottees had a sufficient common interest and grievance; their separate causes of action did not make the procedure unavailable.
issues.legal_principle: Order I, Rule 8 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, serves the public interest by avoiding multiplicity of litigation. Its essential requirement is sameness of interest, shown by a common interest or a common grievance; the court should assess whether there is sufficient community of interest to justify the procedure. In Kodia Goundar v. Velandi Goundar, ILR 1955 Madras 339, the Full Bench emphasized sameness of interest and an interpretation that advances the rule's purpose. The Explanation to Order I, Rule 8, added by the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Act, 1976, clarifies that represented persons need not have the same cause of action.

rule.if: representative_suit and same_scheme_and_material_facts and common_basis_for_challenge and (common_interest or common_grievance)

predicates.representative_suit: One or more persons brought a suit on behalf of a larger group of persons.
predicates.same_scheme_and_material_facts: The represented persons' relevant circumstances arose under the same scheme and shared materially common facts.
predicates.common_basis_for_challenge: The challenged conduct rested on a basis applicable to the represented persons, and the representative's plea was available to them.
predicates.common_interest: The represented persons shared an interest in the matter the suit sought to resolve.
predicates.common_grievance: The represented persons shared a grievance that the suit sought to redress.

issues.definition: A representative suit is maintainable when the represented group shares materially common circumstances and a basis for challenging the conduct, together with a common interest or grievance, even if individual causes of action differ.
